members.statement_original:
In order to present our uniform results on testing, we require some conventions for probabilistic notation used in what follows. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable space equipped with a family of probability measures $(\mathbb P_P)_{P\in\mathcal P}$ where $\mathcal P$ is a collection of distributions on a Euclidean space. We will permit the family $\mathcal P$ to depend on $n$, to allow for settings where the number of parameters grows with $n$, but will typically suppress this in the notation. Given a family of sequences of random variables $(X_{P,n})_{P\in\mathcal P,n\in\mathbb N}$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ whose distributions are determined by $P\in\mathcal P$, we write $X_{P,n}=o_{\mathcal P}(1)$ if $\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb P_P(|X_{P,n}|>\epsilon)\to0$ for every $\epsilon>0$. Similarly, we write $X_{P,n}=O_{\mathcal P}(1)$ if, for any $\epsilon>0$, there exist $M_\epsilon,N_\epsilon>0$ such that $\sup_{n\ge N_\epsilon}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb P_P(|X_{P,n}|>M_\epsilon)<\epsilon$.
In addition, for another family of sequences of random variables $(Y_{P,n})_{P\in\mathcal P,n\in\mathbb N}$, we write $X_{P,n}=o_{\mathcal P}(Y_{P,n})$ if there exists $R_{P,n}$ with $X_{P,n}=Y_{P,n}R_{P,n}$ and $R_{P,n}=o_{\mathcal P}(1)$; likewise, we write $X_{P,n}=O_{\mathcal P}(Y_{P,n})$ if $R_{P,n}=O_{\mathcal P}(1)$ in this representation. We say that $(X_{P,n})_{P\in\mathcal P,n\in\mathbb N}$ converges uniformly in distribution to random variable $X$ with distribution function $F$ if for all continuity points $x$ of $F$, we have
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}|\mathbb P_P(X_{P,n}\le x)-F(x)|=0.
\]

members.local_label: Algorithm 1 — Projected Covariance Measure: single sample split
members.source_heading: Algorithm 1 — Projected Covariance Measure: single sample split
members.statement_original:
Input: Data $(X_i,Y_i,Z_i)_{i=1}^{2n}$, significance level $\alpha\in(0,1)$, partition of $[2n]=\mathcal I_1\cup\mathcal I_2$ into index sets $\mathcal I_1$ and $\mathcal I_2$, each of size $n$.
Options: Regression methods for each of the regressions.
Define: $\mathcal D_j=(X_i,Y_i,Z_i)_{i\in\mathcal I_j}$ for $j\in[2]$.
1: Form $\hat h$.
(i) Regress $Y$ onto $(X,Z)$ using $\mathcal D_2$ to give fitted regression function $\hat g$.
(ii) If $\hat g$ can be modified so that all components involving only $Z$ are set to $0$, let $\tilde g$ be this modified version of $\hat g$. Alternatively, set $\tilde g:=\hat g$.
(iii) Regress $\tilde g(X,Z)$ onto $Z$ using $\mathcal D_2$ to give fitted regression function $\tilde m$, and then set $\tilde h(x,z):=\tilde g(x,z)-\tilde m(z)$.
(iv) Compute
\[
\hat\rho:=\frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_2}\{Y_i-\hat g(X_i,Z_i)+\tilde g(X_i,Z_i)-\tilde m(Z_i)\}\tilde h(X_i,Z_i),
\]
and set $\hat h(x,z):=\operatorname{sgn}(\hat\rho)\tilde h(x,z)$,
2: Form $\hat v$.
(i) Regress $\{Y-\hat g(X,Z)\}^2$ onto $(X,Z)$ using $\mathcal D_2$ to give $\tilde v$.
(ii) Define $a:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$ by
\[
a(c):=\frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_2}\frac{\{Y_i-\hat g(X_i,Z_i)\}^2}{\max\{\tilde v(X_i,Z_i),0\}+c}.
\]
If $a(0)\le1$, set $\hat c:=0$; otherwise find $\hat c$ by solving $a(c)=1$. Set $\hat v(x,z):=\max\{\tilde v(x,z),0\}+\hat c$.
3: Compute test statistic.
(i) Set $\hat f(x,z):=\hat h(x,z)/\hat v(x,z)$ and regress $\hat f(X,Z)$ onto $Z$ using $\mathcal D_1$, giving $\hat m_{\hat f}$.
(ii) Regress $Y$ onto $Z$ using $\mathcal D_1$ to give $\hat m$.
(iii) For $i\in\mathcal I_1$ set $L_i:=\{Y_i-\hat m(Z_i)\}\{\hat f(X_i,Z_i)-\hat m_{\hat f}(Z_i)\}$ and let
\[
T:=\frac{\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}L_i}{\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}L_i^2-\left(\frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}L_i\right)^2}}.
\]
4: Reject $H_0$ if $T>z_{1-\alpha}$.

members.statement_original: Throughout this section, we assume that $(X,Z)\in[0,1]^{d_X}\times[0,1]^{d_Z}$ and set $d:=d_X+d_Z$. In Section S4, we give a self-contained description of spline spaces and their tensor product B-spline bases, containing all the results that we require for our analysis. Given a spline order $r\in\mathbb N$ (i.e. degree $r-1$) and $N\in\mathbb N_0$ equi-spaced interior knots in each dimension, we denote by $\mathcal S^{d_Z}_{r,N}$ the corresponding spline space on $[0,1]^{d_Z}$, and by $\phi^Z$ its $d_Z$-tensor B-spline basis, which consists of $K_Z:=(N+r)^{d_Z}$ basis functions. Writing $\mathcal S^{d_X}_{r,N}$ for the corresponding spline space on $[0,1]^{d_X}$ with $d_X$-tensor B-spline basis $\phi^X$, having $K_X:=(N+r)^{d_X}$ basis functions, we can define the $d$-tensor product basis $\phi(x,z):=\phi^X(x)\otimes\phi^Z(z)$ for $\mathcal S^d_{r,N}$, where $u\otimes v:=\operatorname{vec}(uv^\top)$, having $K_{XZ}:=K_XK_Z$ basis functions. Further, we let $\psi$ denote the tensor product B-spline basis for $\mathcal S^{d_Z}_{2r-1,N}$, and write $\tilde K_Z:=(N+2r-1)^{d_Z}$; the higher order of the spline basis functions that make up $\psi$ affords better approximation properties that turn out to be useful for our theory.

members.statement_original:
Let $\mathcal P$ be a class of distributions of $(X,Y,Z)$ on $[0,1]^{d_X}\times\mathbb R\times[0,1]^{d_Z}$, and for $P\in\mathcal P$, let $g_P(x,z):=\mathbb E_P(Y\mid X=x,Z=z)$. Assume that there exist $C\ge1$ and $c\in(0,1]$ with the following properties:
(a) For each $P\in\mathcal P$, we have $\mathbb E_P(\varepsilon_P^2\mid X,Z)\ge c$ and there exists $\delta\in(0,2]$ such that $\mathbb E_P(|\varepsilon_P|^{2+\delta}\mid X,Z)\le C$.
(b) For each $P\in\mathcal P$, the marginal distribution of $(X,Z)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]^d$, with density $p_P$ satisfying $\sup_{(x,z)\in[0,1]^d}p_P(x,z)\le C$ and $\inf_{(x,z)\in[0,1]^d}p_P(x,z)\ge c$.
(c) Let $s\in(0,r]$ and let $p_{X\mid Z,P}(\cdot\mid z)$ denote the conditional density of $X$ given $Z=z$. Assume that for all $P\in\mathcal P$, we have $p_{X\mid Z,P}(x\mid\cdot)\in \mathcal H^{d_Z}_s$ for all $x\in[0,1]^{d_X}$, and that $m_P\in \mathcal H^{d_Z}_s$ and $g_P\in \mathcal H^d_s$, with
\[
\max\left\{\sup_{x\in[0,1]^{d_X}}\|p_{X\mid Z,P}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal H_s},\|m_P\|_{\mathcal H_s},\|g_P\|_{\mathcal H_s}\right\}\le C.
\]

members.statement_original: It is interesting to compare this to the conditional independence null $Y\perp\!\!\!\perp X\mid Z$, which has attracted much attention in recent years. The latter asks not just for the regression function to be expressed as a function of $Z$ alone, but in fact for the entire conditional distribution of $Y$ given $(X,Z)$ to equal the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $Z$.
